newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Union to hold 24-hour strikes in W.Australia mines.
newsitem.headline: Union to hold 24-hour strikes in W.Australia mines.

text.p: The Australian Workers Union on Monday began a series of 24-hour strikes strikes in the Western Australia's mining industry to protest against changes to the state's industrial relations laws.

The campaign began at the Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd's iron ore plant at Port Hedland and will spread to other mining operations in the Pilbara region later in the week, AWU secretary Tim Daly told Reuters.
"The Goldfields will stop next week," Daly said.
"We expect virtually the whole of the Goldfields to stop except for Western Mining Corporation. They contracted out their operations 12 months ago," Daly said.
Daly said the AWU was the biggest union in Western Australia's mining industry with 4,000-5,000 members, most of whom work on various iron ore operations in the Pilbara.
He said the 24-hour stoppage at BHP's Port Hedland operation was unlikely to affect production because of a continuity of supply agreement between the union and the company.
"But we expect the stoppages will cause major disruption in the mining industry generally," Daly said. "BHP is the only one we have a continuity of supply agreement with," he said.
Daly said the campaign would continue indefinitely.

The Labour Relations Legislation Amendment Act passed through state parliament last week after the government guillotined further debate. However, it will not become law for another three months because of the government's intention to conduct an information campaign beforehand.

In Monday's West Australian newspaper, the Trades and Labour Council (TLC), which is co-ordinating the protest campaign against the legislation, was quoted as saying unions would seek wage rises of up to A$150 a week to make up for the restrictions imposed on the workers' ability to improve wages and living standards. The TLC has also signalled its intention to launch international and legal challenges to the legislation.
